opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'm a bit skeptical of the idea that you need a separate, dedicated model just for synthetic data. The way I see it, the best synthetic data generator is usually just your best model. If you have a strong general model, it's already good at writing, reasoning, coding, and following instructions, and those are exactly the skills you need to produce high-quality training data. Building a separate, specialized "data model" can end up as a detour where you invest a lot of effort in something that falls behind your frontier model a few months later.

What I do think matters a lot is the pipeline around generation, not so much a dedicated generator. For Llama, a huge part of post-training was synthetic: the model generates candidates, then you filter with reward models, execution feedback for code, verifiers for math, rejection sampling, and so on. The value is in that loop: generate, verify, select, retrain, and repeat. Each iteration the model gets better, so the data it produces gets better, and you bootstrap. If you freeze a separate model whose only job is generating data, you lose some of that self-improvement dynamic.

There is a nuance, though. For some domains, specialization does help. If you need, say, very specific long-context data, tool-use trajectories, or a particular language that's underrepresented, it can make sense to fine-tune a variant, or build an expert, that's especially good at producing that slice of data, and then distill it back into the general model. We did things in that spirit: train an expert on code, use it to generate and filter data, and feed that into the main model. So I'd frame it less as "dedicated synthetic data models" and more as "temporary experts in service of the main model."

The other point people underestimate is that the bottleneck is increasingly verification rather than generation. Generating a million samples is cheap now. Knowing which ten thousand are actually correct, diverse, and useful is the hard part. So if I had to invest in a dedicated model, I'd probably rather invest in better judges and reward models than in a pure generator.

And longer term, I think we're moving toward models surpassing human annotators on many tasks. Humans are still very valuable for comparing outputs and saying which one is better, even when they couldn't write the best answer themselves. That's the beauty of RLHF. But for actually writing the data, the model is often already better than the average annotator. So synthetic data isn't a niche trick; it's becoming the default. I just don't think it requires a separate species of model to get there.

r001.rationale: The response says the best synthetic data generator is usually the strongest model and that as the model improves, the data it produces improves too.

r002.rationale: It describes training domain experts to generate data and distilling them into the main model, but does not identify larger models that are not used for inference as justified by this approach.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a really interesting question, and honestly I've changed my mind on it over time. When we were doing Llama 2 and then Llama 3, a huge fraction of the post-training data was synthetic. People think of synthetic data as a shortcut, but in practice it became the main lever. The quality of what you can generate is bounded by the model you generate with, so the question becomes: do you want one general model that also happens to generate data, or a model you train specifically to be good at producing training signal?

My view is that the second is underrated. If you look at what you actually need from a data generator, it's not the same thing you need from a chat assistant. You want diversity, you want coverage of the long tail, you want the ability to produce hard examples, and you want it to be calibrated about when something is correct. A chat model is optimized to give one safe, helpful answer. That's almost the opposite of what you want when you're trying to cover the distribution. So a dedicated generator, or a family of them, with a different objective, makes a lot of sense to me.

The other piece is verification. The thing that made synthetic data work for us wasn't just generation, it was rejection sampling, it was having rewards, execution for code, checkers for math. A generator paired with a strong verifier is a much more defensible pipeline than just asking the biggest model to produce more text. And once you frame it that way, the generator doesn't even need to be the most capable model. It needs to be cheap, diverse, and good at exploring, and you let the verifier do the filtering.

The risk people raise is model collapse, that you train on your own outputs and degrade. I think that's real if you do it naively, but it's mostly an argument against closed loops without any external signal. If you have a verifier, or humans in the loop on the hard cases, or you ground in real world data for some fraction, it's fine. We saw improvements, not collapse.

So yes, I'm fairly bullish. I think in a couple of years we'll look at "the model" as actually a system of models, and some of them will exist purely to teach the others. That's already happening inside the big labs, it's just not something people talk about as a product.

r001.rationale: It says generated-data quality is bounded by the model used to generate it, communicating that the generator’s capability limits data quality.

r002.rationale: It describes dedicated generators that teach other models, but does not identify distilling specific knowledge as a reason to use larger models that are not used for inference.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a strong case for it, because generating useful training data is a different objective from being a good assistant. As an assistant, you want to give the best answer you can. As a data generator, you want to produce examples that help another model learn. Those aren’t necessarily the same thing.

For example, a generator that produces only easy, perfectly correct examples might be less useful than one that targets things the student is struggling with. So I’d want to evaluate it by training on its output and measuring whether the student improves, rather than just judging how good the generated text looks.

The challenge is that you can generate an enormous amount of data without adding much information. You need diversity, a useful level of difficulty, and some way to check correctness. If you can close that loop—generate, train, evaluate, and use the results to improve the generator—then a dedicated model becomes very interesting.

r001.rationale: The response argues for a dedicated data generator, but does not say generation improves as the model becomes more capable.

r002.rationale: It discusses creating training data and improving a student, but does not identify distilling specific knowledge or justify larger models that are not used for inference.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a strong case for it, because generating useful training data is a different objective from answering a user’s question. As a user, you want the best answer. For training, you want examples that help the next model learn something it doesn’t already know.

So the best generator isn’t necessarily just the strongest general-purpose model. You could optimize it to produce diverse problems, target weaknesses in the model you’re training, and generate answers that you can verify. The important thing is the learning signal, not how impressive the generated text looks.

But you need a feedback loop. If you just generate more and more text and train on it, there’s no guarantee you improve. You have to measure whether that data actually makes the next model better. That’s where a dedicated model becomes interesting: you can optimize the generation process for that improvement.

r001.rationale: The response says a generator need not be the strongest general-purpose model and emphasizes optimizing for useful learning signals; it does not state that synthetic data improves as the generating model becomes more capable.

r002.rationale: The response discusses dedicated generation models but does not identify distilling specific knowledge or justify larger models that are not used for inference.
